unit.title: Acquire foundation knowledge of massage therapy

summary: This unit gives you the foundation knowledge for massage: what massage is and what it does to the body, the parts of the body you work on, the consultation, contraindications and informed consent, professional manner and hygiene, preparing the room, couch and mediums, safe posture, draping and positioning the client, the five classic massage movements, and aftercare and records.

blocks.p: Massage is one of the most requested treatments in spas, hotels and salons. Clients ask for it to relax, to ease tight muscles and to feel better. This unit gives you the **foundation knowledge** you need before you give a massage: how it works, who must not be massaged, how to protect the client's dignity, how to protect your own body, and what the basic movements are. It is for GENERAL BEAUTY THERAPY LEVEL 2 trainees.

A good massage is safe, private and professional as well as pleasant. A massage given to the wrong client, or in the wrong way, can cause real harm. So you learn **when not to massage** and **how to behave** before you learn the strokes.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's treatment room: a role play of the consultation, consent and draping, and a short massage with the five groups of movements, given to a partner who agrees. The assessor watches your safety, consent, draping, posture and manner, not only the strokes.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, practise draping over clothing only. Use made-up client details, not real health information. Photograph only the couch, towels, forms and hands, never faces.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What massage is and what it does

blocks.p: **Massage** is the use of the hands on the skin and the soft tissues (muscles and the tissues around them) in set ways, with different pressures, to relax, to ease tension and to improve wellbeing. It is a **treatment of touch**: it works by moving the tissues, warming them and stimulating the nerves. It is not a cure for illness.

**Swedish massage**, the style behind the classic movements, uses stroking, kneading, striking, small deep circles and shaking, usually with oil on bare skin. Other styles from around the world are covered in the unit on the history of massage.

head: Body part
Effects of massage
rows: Skin
Loosens and removes dead skin cells
Brings more blood to the surface; the skin looks pinker and warmer
Oil softens the skin; the sebaceous glands and sweat glands may work more
Muscles
Warms the muscles and makes them more flexible
Eases stiffness and tension; relaxes tight muscles
Helps remove waste products by moving blood and lymph through them
Circulation
Widens the small blood vessels and increases blood flow to the area
Helps blood return to the heart through the veins, so that more oxygen and nutrients reach the tissues
Lymphatic system
Helps lymph to move towards the lymph nodes
Helps waste to be carried away and may reduce puffiness
Nervous system
Slow, rhythmic strokes soothe the nerves and relax
Brisk movements stimulate
Mind
Calms and reduces stress; many clients sleep better
The attention and care of the therapist add to the effect

blocks.note: Be honest about what massage can do. It can relax and ease tight muscles, and it may help someone feel better. It does not cure illness, and a therapist never claims it does. If a client has pain you do not understand, advise her to see a doctor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Beauty therapists give massage in salons, spas and hotels, usually on a couch in a private treatment room. A back, neck and shoulder massage takes about 30 minutes; a full-body massage usually takes about an hour. Work only in a clean, private room with a couch, towels and proper hygiene, never in a place where privacy, cleanliness and consent cannot be kept.

sections.title: Know the body: skin, bones, muscles, circulation and lymph

blocks.p: You do not need to learn the whole body, but you need to know what lies under your hands: where the muscles are, where the bones are close to the skin (where you must be gentle), which way blood and lymph flow, and where the lymph nodes are.

head: Layer
What it is
Why it matters in massage
rows: Epidermis
The thin outer layer of the skin; its top cells are dead and are shed all the time.
Massage loosens the dead cells.
Dermis
The layer under the epidermis, with blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, sebaceous glands and hair follicles.
Where touch, pressure and warmth are sensed and where blood flow increases.
Subcutaneous layer (under the dermis)
A layer of fat and connective tissue over the muscles.
The tissue you move when you knead and press.

ul: The **vertebral column** (spine) is the column of bones down the middle of the back: 7 neck (cervical), 12 chest (thoracic) and 5 lower back (lumbar) vertebrae, then the sacrum and the coccyx. It protects the spinal cord. **Never press or strike directly on the spine.**
The **scapula** (shoulder blade) and the **clavicle** (collarbone) form the shoulder. The **humerus** is the upper arm bone.
The **ribs** protect the chest; under the lowest ribs, at the back, lie the **kidneys**: this is the **kidney area**, and no tapotement is used there.
Bony areas such as the knees, ankles, elbows, hips and the spine are only stroked lightly: do not press hard on them.

head: Muscle
Where it is
What it does
rows: Trapezius
A large diamond-shaped muscle across the upper back and the back of the neck
Moves the shoulders and the head; often tight in people who work at desks
Deltoid
Covers the shoulder joint
Lifts the arm
Latissimus dorsi
A large, flat muscle on each side of the middle and lower back
Pulls the arm down and back
Erector spinae
Long muscles that run up each side of the spine
Hold the back upright and bend it backwards
Rhomboids
Between the shoulder blade and the spine
Pull the shoulder blades together
Gluteals
The buttock muscles
Move the hip and hold the body upright
Biceps and triceps
Front and back of the upper arm
Bend and straighten the elbow
Pectoralis major
The chest
Moves the arm across the body
Quadriceps
The front of the thigh
Straighten the knee
Hamstrings
The back of the thigh
Bend the knee
Gastrocnemius
The calf, at the back of the lower leg
Lifts the heel; pushes off when walking
Sternocleidomastoid
The side of the neck, from behind the ear to the collarbone
Turns and tilts the head

ul: **Arteries** carry blood away from the heart. **Veins** carry blood back to the heart. Veins have one-way valves, which stop blood flowing backwards, and they depend on muscle movement to push blood on.
Because veins return blood to the heart, firm massage strokes on the limbs are done **towards the heart**, to help the blood in the veins. The return stroke is light.
A **blood clot** in a deep vein (**deep vein thrombosis**, or DVT) can break off and travel to the lungs, which can be fatal. That is why you never massage a limb that may have a clot.
**Lymph** is a clear fluid that drains waste and extra fluid from the tissues and helps the body fight infection. It flows one way, through lymph vessels, to **lymph nodes** and back to the blood.
Large groups of lymph nodes are in the **neck**, the **armpits**, the **groin**, and behind the knees. Do not press hard on them.
Massage towards the nearest group of nodes helps lymph to flow and may reduce puffiness.

blocks.p: The **nervous system** is the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves. The nerve endings in the skin sense touch, pressure and warmth. Slow strokes calm the nervous system and brisk strokes stimulate it. Pressure that causes pain is not relaxing and can cause harm: always check the pressure with the client.
The consultation is a private conversation before the massage. You find out what the client wants and whether it is safe to treat her, agree the plan and record it. Do it before she undresses.

flow: Greet the client in private and explain what will happen
Ask about her health, medicines, allergies and goals
Check for contraindications
Decide: treat, avoid an area, or refer
Agree the areas, the pressure and the time
Explain draping and that she can stop at any time
Get informed consent and her signature

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants: relaxation, a sore back, a time limit
Plans the areas, the pressure and the pace.
Health: heart, blood pressure, diabetes, epilepsy, asthma, cancer, blood clots, recent surgery, pregnancy
Some conditions stop the massage; some need a doctor's approval.
Medicines, including blood thinners and painkillers
Blood thinners make bruising easy; painkillers may hide pain you would otherwise feel.
Allergies: nuts, oils, creams, latex
To choose a safe medium and avoid a reaction.
Injuries, pain, scars or skin problems
Areas to avoid or treat gently.
Recent food, alcohol or drugs
A heavy meal, alcohol or drugs make a massage unsafe or uncomfortable.
Whether she has had a massage before
She may need more explanation.

blocks.p: A **contraindication** is a condition that means the massage must not go ahead, or must be changed. Think of three kinds.

head: Kind
What it means
Examples
rows: Total: do not massage at all that day
Massage could spread infection or harm her.
Fever or a high temperature (this includes illness such as flu, dengue or chikungunya)
Infectious or contagious conditions, including skin infections
Under the influence of alcohol or drugs
Recent operation
Blood clot or suspected clot (DVT)
Severe pain with no known cause
A heavy meal just eaten
Local: avoid that area and massage the rest
Massage on the area could cause pain or harm.
Cuts, grazes or open wounds
Bruises
Sunburn
Recent scars
Swelling or inflamed areas
Varicose veins
Boils, rashes or sores
Undiagnosed lumps
A recent fracture or sprain
Needs a doctor's approval first
Massage may be safe, but a doctor must decide.
Heart conditions
High or low blood pressure
Diabetes
Epilepsy
Cancer or treatment for cancer
Pregnancy
Sickle cell disease
Osteoporosis
Taking blood thinners
Kidney problems

ul: **Why a blood clot is a total contraindication:** massage may move the clot, and a clot that travels to the lungs can kill.
**Why alcohol is:** it widens blood vessels and affects judgement and pain; the client may not feel if the pressure is too much, and may feel faint.
**Why fever is:** the body is fighting infection, and massage could spread it and make the client worse. It also puts you and other clients at risk.
**Varicose veins:** do not press over them or massage them; the veins are weak and may be damaged or may hold a clot.

**A client with a heart condition, high blood pressure, diabetes or pregnancy:** ask for her doctor's approval, in writing if the Centre requires it, before you treat her. Pregnancy needs special training and approval.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Never diagnose, never tell the client she has a disease, and never promise that massage will help a medical condition. Explain tactfully why you cannot treat her today, advise her to see a doctor, record it on the card and keep it private.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: In Jamaica, high blood pressure, diabetes and sickle cell disease are common, and fevers from dengue and chikungunya do occur. Ask every client about them, and do not treat anyone with a fever. Clients may also use tablets for blood pressure or blood sugar: ask.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Informed consent** means the client understands the treatment (what you will do, the areas, undressing and draping, the oil and any risks) and agrees to it, freely. She signs the form.

ul: A client **under 18** needs her parent's or guardian's consent. Follow the Centre's rules about whether the parent must stay in the room.
Tell her she can **stop the massage at any time**, for any reason. If she asks you to stop, stop at once and ask if she is all right.
Check consent again if you change what you planned.
Never carry on if she says no, or if she looks uncomfortable.
Date, name, contact details and age.
Health, medicines, allergies; contraindications found and the decision made.
Areas treated, the oil or cream used and the pressure.
Reactions, advice given, the date of the next visit, and the price in JMD.
Her **signature** and the date. Keep the card locked away: under Jamaica's Data Protection Act, health details are personal information and must be kept private and secure.

head: Area
What a professional therapist does
rows: Appearance
Clean, ironed uniform and closed, comfortable shoes
Short, clean nails; hair tied back
No loose jewellery; no strong perfume
Manner
On time, polite and calm
Explains clearly and speaks in a quiet voice
Keeps the talk to the treatment: no gossip, no personal problems, no complaining about other clients
Boundaries
Treats only the areas agreed, with the client draped
No improper comments or touch
Stops when the client asks
Confidentiality
Never discusses a client's health or body with others
Keeps records locked away
Working within her training
Does not diagnose or treat illness
Refers to a doctor
Does not use a technique she has not been trained in
Honesty
Does not make false claims; gives true prices; admits mistakes

blocks.note: A therapist who is rude, careless or who crosses a boundary harms the client and the good name of massage. If a client makes you uncomfortable or asks for something improper, stay calm, end the treatment politely and tell your supervisor.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Wash your hands** with soap and water before and after every client. Cover any cuts on your hands with a waterproof plaster.
Keep your nails short and your uniform clean.
Use a **fresh towel and fresh couch roll** for every client. Put used towels in a closed laundry bin and wash them hot.
Wipe the couch, the face cradle and the equipment with disinfectant after each client, and let it dry.
Take oil from a **pump bottle**, or pour a little into a clean bowl, so that the stock bottle is not contaminated. Never dip your hand into a big bottle or tub.
Check the client's skin for infection before you start; do not treat an infection.
Put waste in a lidded bin. Keep the room clean and ventilated.

sections.title: The room, couch, mediums and your posture

ul: **Warm** enough for a client with little clothing: about 22 to 25 degrees Celsius is comfortable. In Jamaica, air conditioning can make a room too cold: set it so she is not shivering, and have extra towels.
**Quiet**, with soft lighting and relaxing music at a low volume if the Centre allows it.
**Clean and private**: door closed or lockable, curtains or blinds drawn, a place to undress, a hook or chair for clothes.
**Ventilated**, with a lidded bin, tissues and a jug of water with a cup.
Check everything before the client arrives.
Check it is stable and that the legs and any adjustable parts are locked.
Set it at the right **height for you**: when you stand beside it, you should be able to work with a straight back and relaxed shoulders, without bending over.
Wipe it with disinfectant and cover it with fresh couch roll and a clean towel; have a spare towel for warmth and for draping.
Have supports ready: a bolster or rolled towel for under the ankles and the knees, a small pillow, and a face cradle for the client lying face down.
Have a small step for clients who need help to get on.

blocks.p: A **medium** is the oil, cream or powder that lets your hands glide over the skin without pulling it.

head: Medium
What it is
Take care
rows: Massage oil (for example sweet almond, grapeseed, coconut)
Plant oil that lets the hands glide for a long time.
Check for allergy first. Sweet almond oil can cause a reaction in a client with a nut allergy. Coconut oil goes solid when it is cool: warm it in your hands.
Cream or lotion
A water-based medium that is absorbed more quickly.
Less slip; may need topping up. Check for allergy.
Talc or powder
Used to reduce friction on very hairy skin or when a dry feel is wanted.
Dust can irritate the airways; keep it light.
Essential oils (in a carrier oil)
Aromatherapy; they are strong and can irritate.
Used only if you are trained, and only as the maker says. Ask about allergies, asthma and pregnancy.

ul: **Ask about allergies before you use any oil.** Never use a product the client says she is allergic to.
Use only a little oil. Warm a little in your hands, then add more as needed. Cold oil poured straight on the skin is uncomfortable.
Keep oil away from the eyes and from broken skin.
Wipe up any oil that spills on the floor at once: it is a slip hazard.

blocks.p: Therapists often get back, neck, shoulder, wrist and thumb pain. Good posture protects you and gives a better massage, because you can use your body weight rather than tired arms.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Set the couch at the right height so that your back stays straight
Bend over a couch that is too low
Stand with your **feet apart**, knees slightly bent (soft), and your weight over both feet
Stand with locked knees or your feet together
Move your **body weight** forward and back from your legs, so that your arms stay relaxed
Push with the strength of your arms and thumbs alone
Keep your wrists straight and your shoulders relaxed
Hunch your shoulders or bend your wrists sharply
**Walk round** the couch to reach the other side
Stretch across the client
Take breaks, stretch your hands, drink water
Work for hours without a break

blocks.note: Use the large, flat parts of your hands and your body weight for pressure. Use your thumbs sparingly, because they tire easily and can be injured.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Position
What it means
Supports
rows: Prone
Lying **face down**: used for the back, the back of the legs and the shoulders
A rolled towel or bolster under the **ankles**, to ease the lower back and the feet
A face cradle, or a pillow, and the head turned to one side if there is no cradle
Arms by the sides or under the head
Supine
Lying **face up**: used for the front of the legs, the arms, the neck and the face
A bolster or rolled towel under the **knees**, to ease the lower back
A small pillow under the head
Semi-reclined
Lying with the head and chest raised
For clients who cannot lie flat, for example with breathing difficulty or late pregnancy (only with approval)

blocks.p: **Draping** is covering the client with towels so that only the area being worked on is uncovered. It keeps the client **warm**, protects her **privacy and dignity**, helps her relax and shows a professional manner.

blocks.h: How to drape for a back massage

flow: Explain what you will do, and what she should wear (underwear usually stays on)
Leave the room, or turn away, while she undresses and gets under the towel, lying face down
Come back after you knock, and ask if she is comfortable
Uncover only the back, tucking the towel securely at the sides and at the hips
Keep her private areas covered at all times
Cover the back and uncover the next area before you move on; use an extra towel over the legs for warmth

ul: Hold the towel up between you and the client when you move it, so that nothing is seen.
Never uncover an area until you have explained it and she has agreed.
Keep the towel tucked in, so that it does not slip. Check regularly.
To work on a leg, uncover only that leg and tuck the towel round the thigh; for the arms, uncover one arm at a time.
Do not uncover the chest, the breasts or the genital area.

blocks.note: Draping is the same for every client. A client who is shy, unwell, older or from a culture or faith with strict ideas about modesty needs especially careful draping and a calm explanation. If she asks for the towel to be tucked more or for another area to stay covered, do as she asks.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, you practise draping with the 'client' fully clothed. No one undresses for the task. Help the partner on and off the couch, using the step if needed.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Classic (Swedish) massage uses **five groups of movements**. A massage usually starts and ends with effleurage and uses the others in between. Always check the pressure with the client, and never cause pain.

head: Movement
What it is
Main effects
Cautions
rows: Effleurage
Long, smooth, gliding strokes with the whole hand or the thumbs. Firmer on the way towards the heart, light on the return.
Spreads the oil
Warms and relaxes the tissues
Helps blood and lymph flow
Links the other movements; used at the start and end
Keep the hand moulded to the body. On the limbs, firm pressure goes towards the heart.
Petrissage
Kneading, squeezing and lifting the muscles: includes kneading, wringing, picking up and skin rolling.
Loosens and stretches the muscles
Helps the blood and lymph flow and removes waste
Eases tension
Lift the muscle gently away from the bone; do not pinch the skin.
Friction
Small, deep circles with the thumbs or fingertips, in one spot, moving the skin over the tissue under it.
Loosens knots and tight spots
Warms a small area
Breaks down tension around joints
Use sparingly. Not over bruises or broken skin.
Tapotement (percussion)
Quick, light striking movements: hacking, cupping, beating, pounding, tapping and plucking.
Stimulates the nerves and the circulation
Tones the muscle
**Never** over bony areas, the spine, the kidney area, varicose veins, bruises or a client who is frail or has high blood pressure.
Vibration
A fine shaking or trembling given by the hands, either held in one place or sliding along.
Stimulates or soothes the nerves
May ease tension
Light; not over painful areas.

flow: Effleurage to spread the oil and warm the area
Petrissage to work into the muscles
Friction on tight spots, if needed
Tapotement or vibration to stimulate, if suitable
Effleurage to finish and calm the area

ul: Start light and build up. Ask the client, 'Is this pressure all right?' and adjust.
Keep one hand in contact with the client whenever you can, so that the massage feels smooth.
Keep a steady, slow, rhythmic pace for relaxation. Brisk movements stimulate.
Never press on the spine, the lymph nodes, the front of the neck or a bony area.
Stop at once if the client feels pain, dizziness or asks you to stop.
On the **limbs**, firm strokes go **towards the heart**, to help blood in the veins and lymph.
On the **back**, strokes usually go up along each side of the spine towards the shoulders and out and back down lightly.
On the **neck and shoulders**, strokes go from the neck out over the shoulders.

blocks.note: In practical work, give your partner a short massage on the back (draped, face down) or the forearm and hand (clothed). Use all five movements, check pressure, keep tapotement off the spine, bones and the kidney area, and ask about nut and other allergies before using any oil.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Finish with slow effleurage
Tell the client the massage is finished, softly
Leave the room while she sits up slowly and dresses
Offer water
Ask how she feels
Give aftercare advice
Record the treatment

blocks.p: Some clients feel light-headed when they sit up, because blood pressure drops when they move from lying flat. Help her sit up **slowly**, let her sit for a moment before she stands, give her water, and stay with her until she is steady.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Drink water
Helps the body to flush out waste and replaces fluid.
Rest and take it easy
The body is relaxed; rest helps the benefits to last.
Avoid alcohol, a heavy meal and hard exercise for a while
The circulation is stimulated and the muscles are relaxed.
Avoid very hot baths or saunas straight after
Too much heat on top of the massage can make her feel faint.
Report any pain, rash or other problem
So that you can deal with it, and refer her if needed.
Book regular massages if she wants
A single massage helps, but regular ones help more.

blocks.p: A **contra-action** is an unwanted reaction during or after a treatment. A **contraindication** is something that stops a treatment. Do not confuse them.

head: Reaction
What to do
rows: Light-headedness or dizziness
Help her sit up slowly; give water; stay with her until steady.
Tiredness or sleepiness
Normal; advise rest; advise her not to drive if she feels drowsy.
Headache
Give water; advise rest; check ventilation.
Soreness or stiffness the next day
May happen after deep work; advise light movement and water; use lighter pressure next time.
Needing the toilet
Allow her to go; normal after massage.
Feeling emotional or tearful
Stay calm and kind; give time and water; do not pry.
Skin reaction: redness, itching, rash
Remove the oil with a warm damp towel; stop using that product; record it and refer if it does not settle.
Nausea, severe pain or breathing difficulty
Stop; get help; call for medical help if serious.

ul: Record every reaction and what you did.
If a reaction does not settle, advise the client to see her doctor.
Put used towels and couch roll in the laundry bin and waste in the lidded bin.
Wipe the couch, the face cradle and the equipment with disinfectant.
Wipe up any oil on the floor.
Wash your hands, and refill the oil from the stock bottle, not from used oil.
Complete the record card: areas treated, oil used, reactions, advice and next visit.
I can explain what massage is, and what it does to the skin, muscles, circulation, lymph and mind.
I can say honestly what massage cannot do.
I can name the main muscles and bones I work over, and where the kidney area and the lymph nodes are.
I can explain why firm strokes on the limbs go towards the heart.
I can carry out a consultation and ask the right questions.
I can sort contraindications into those that stop the massage, those where I avoid one area and those that need a doctor's approval.
I can explain why a blood clot, a fever and alcohol stop a massage.
I can explain informed consent, and what to do when a client asks me to stop or is under 18.
I can describe a professional manner and name the hygiene steps.
I can prepare the room and the couch, and check for allergies before using oil.
I can stand and move safely to protect my back, shoulders and thumbs.
I can position a client prone and supine with supports.
I can drape a client for a back massage and explain why draping matters.
I can describe the five groups of movements, what each does, and where each must not be used.
I can give aftercare advice, deal with unwanted reactions and keep records.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each point, not only the point. For example: 'I do not use tapotement over the kidney area, because the kidneys lie close to the surface under the lowest ribs and are easily bruised.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The use of the hands on the skin and soft tissues, in set ways, to relax and ease tension.

An oil, cream or powder that helps the hands glide.
Kneading, squeezing and lifting the muscles.

Quick, light striking movements such as hacking and cupping.
A fine shaking or trembling of the hands.
A condition that stops a treatment or means it must be changed.
An unwanted reaction during or after a treatment.
The client understands the treatment and agrees to it.
Covering the client with towels so that only the area worked on is uncovered.
A padded rest with a hole that supports the face when lying face down.
The outer layer of the skin.
The layer of skin under the epidermis, with blood vessels and nerves.
The column of bones down the back (the spine).
The large muscle across the upper back and the back of the neck.
The muscle that covers the shoulder joint.
The large, flat muscle on each side of the middle and lower back.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
A blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart.
A blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg.
The system that carries lymph and helps fight infection.
A small gland that filters lymph; groups are in the neck, armpits and groin.
The brain, spinal cord and nerves.
The lower back under the ribs, where tapotement must never be used.

c1.title: A spa consultation in Negril
c1.text: Mr. Andre Palmer, 47, books a back massage at a hotel spa in Negril. In the consultation he tells trainee Shanique that he has high blood pressure and takes tablets for it, but has not seen his doctor in over a year. He says he had two beers with lunch and a large plate of food half an hour ago. He wants deep, firm pressure because his shoulders are tight.

c2.title: A tight calf in Santa Cruz
c2.text: Mrs. Beverley Thomas, 38, comes to a salon in Santa Cruz for a leg massage. She says her left calf has been tight, swollen, warm and a bit red since a long bus journey two days ago, and it hurts when she walks. She thinks 'a good rub' will loosen it. The other leg looks normal.

c3.title: Draping in Port Antonio
c3.text: At a training spa in Port Antonio, trainee Rojae gives Ms. Alicia Grant a back massage. He explains the treatment, then stays in the room while she undresses. He draws back the whole towel at once to reach her legs, and is chatting about a friend's health problems while he works. Ms. Grant tenses up and says nothing.

c4.title: A tired therapist in Morant Bay
c4.text: Trainee Dennis in Morant Bay gives several massages a day. The couch is low, so he bends over it and presses hard with his thumbs. By the afternoon his lower back and thumbs ache. He uses tapotement over a client's mid-back, down the sides of the spine, and the client winces.

c5.title: Oils and aftercare in Mandeville
c5.text: In Mandeville, trainee Sasha is preparing to massage Mr. Winston Clarke with sweet almond oil. Mr. Clarke has not been asked about allergies. The coconut oil she also has on the trolley has gone solid in the cool room. After a 30-minute back massage, Mr. Clarke sits up quickly, says he feels dizzy and wants to dress and leave.

questions.q: Mr. Palmer says he had two beers half an hour ago. What should Shanique do?
o: Give the massage with lighter pressure and finish a little early
Give a short massage after he has drunk a large glass of water
Wait a few minutes and then begin if he says he feels well
Not treat him today, and explain kindly that he can rebook
questions.why: Alcohol widens blood vessels and can hide pain, so a client who has been drinking is a total contraindication for that day. Explain tactfully and rebook.

questions.q: He also has high blood pressure and has not seen his doctor for a year. What is the best way to deal with this?
o: Ask him to get his doctor's approval before a massage, and record this
Treat him normally, as he is on tablets and so his pressure is controlled
Treat him, but use only light pressure and keep the session short
Take his blood pressure with a cuff and decide for herself
questions.why: High blood pressure needs a doctor's approval before massage. A therapist does not diagnose or judge whether a condition is controlled; the doctor does.

questions.q: He wants deep, firm pressure. How should Shanique decide the pressure when she does treat a client?
o: Use the deepest pressure the client says he can take
Always use the same medium pressure for every client
Start light, build up, and keep asking, and never cause pain
Use hard pressure on the first visit to show the massage is effective
questions.why: Pressure is agreed with the client and checked throughout. Pain tightens muscles and can cause harm, so you build up gradually.

questions.q: What might Mrs. Thomas's calf signs suggest, and what should the trainee do?
o: A muscle strain: stretch and massage it gently for a few minutes
A possible blood clot: do not massage, and send her to a doctor
Poor circulation: massage the calf upwards, towards the heart
A bruise: avoid the calf only and massage the rest of the leg
questions.why: A swollen, warm, red, painful calf after a long journey can mean a deep vein thrombosis. Massage could move the clot to the lungs, so never massage the leg. She should see a doctor at once.

questions.q: Mrs. Thomas insists the other leg is fine and wants it massaged. What should the trainee do?
o: Yes, but only on the right side and with very light strokes
Yes, using very light strokes on both legs, avoiding the sore calf
Only after medical advice, as the cause of her symptoms is not known
Yes, but spending less time on the sore calf than the other leg
questions.why: A suspected clot is a medical matter and she needs a doctor's advice first. The therapist does not decide that the rest of the legs are safe; refer, and rebook after approval.

questions.q: Which wording is best for the trainee to use with Mrs. Thomas?
o: I cannot treat that leg today. Please see a doctor, as it needs checking
You have a blood clot, so you must go to hospital at once
It is probably a strained muscle, so rest it and come back next week
It is nothing to worry about, but I cannot massage it
questions.why: A therapist cannot diagnose. She says what she cannot do, explains that the leg needs checking, and refers the client to a doctor, without naming a disease or giving false comfort.

questions.q: What should Rojae have done about the towel when he moved to the legs?
o: Remove the whole towel at once so that he can see both legs together
Ask the client to hold the towel herself while he works on the legs
Lay the towel loosely over her so that it can be moved quickly
Uncover only the leg being worked on, and keep the rest tucked in
questions.why: Draping means only the area being worked on is uncovered. The rest stays covered, tucked in and secure, for privacy, warmth and dignity.

questions.q: Why did Rojae make a mistake by staying in the room while she undressed?
o: The therapist should always watch the client, in case she falls
The client may feel watched, so he should leave or turn away
It does not matter when the client is another trainee
He should have asked her to undress at home before coming
questions.why: Privacy and dignity come first. The therapist explains, then leaves the room (or turns away) while the client undresses and gets under the towel.

questions.q: Which professional point is broken by chatting about a friend's health problems?
o: Honesty, because she may have made the story up
Punctuality, because chatting makes the treatment run late
Confidentiality, and keeping the talk to the treatment
Hygiene, because talking spreads germs across the client
questions.why: A professional therapist keeps the talk to the treatment and never discusses other people's health. It can also show the client that her own health details could be shared.

questions.q: What should Dennis change first to avoid his back pain?
o: Press with his thumbs and wrists bent, to save his shoulders
Stretch across the couch so that he does not have to walk round it
Set the couch at a height that lets him work with a straight back
Use lighter pressure on every client so his hands tire less
questions.why: A couch that is too low forces a bent back. Set the height so that he can work with a straight back and relaxed shoulders, then use body weight rather than arm strength.

questions.q: Which stance protects a therapist best during a long day?
o: Feet apart, soft knees, weight moving between the legs
Feet together, knees locked, and leaning over the client
One foot raised on a stool, and weight on the other leg
Standing on tiptoe so that she can reach across the couch
questions.why: A stable stance, with feet apart, soft knees and weight shifting from the legs, lets you use body weight for pressure and spares the back, shoulders and thumbs.

questions.q: Why did the client wince when Dennis used tapotement down the sides of the mid-back?
o: The client was too tense, so the strokes needed to be firmer and slower
The client was ticklish, as the sides of the back often are
Tapotement is suitable only on the legs, never on any part of the back
The kidney area and spine are there, and tapotement avoids both
questions.why: Tapotement is never used over the spine, bones or the kidney area, which lies at the lower back under the ribs. Use it only on thick muscle, lightly, and stop if she is uncomfortable.

questions.q: Which direction should Dennis use for his firm effleurage strokes on a client's arm?
o: Away from the heart, towards the fingers, then back lightly
Towards the heart, with a light return stroke
In small circles round the elbow and wrist joints only
Whichever direction is easiest for him to reach
questions.why: Veins and lymph vessels carry fluid towards the heart, so firm strokes on the limbs go in that direction to help the flow, and the return stroke is light.

questions.q: Mr. Clarke then says that nuts make his lips swell. What should Sasha use instead of the sweet almond oil?
o: A little almond oil mixed with grapeseed oil to weaken it
Almond oil, wiped off the skin after a few minutes
A product with no nut ingredients, checked on its label
Whichever oil he chooses, since oils are all alike
questions.why: A client with a nut allergy must not be given a product with nut oils, even diluted. Read the label of the replacement and keep the allergy on his record card.

questions.q: What is the best way for Sasha to use the solid coconut oil?
o: Melt a small amount between her hands before using it
Stand the whole jar in hot water until all of it is runny
Press a cold lump on the skin and spread it with firm strokes
Leave it out, and use the almond oil without asking
questions.why: Coconut oil goes solid when cool and melts at body warmth. A little warmed in the hands is comfortable and also keeps the stock hygienic.

questions.q: Mr. Clarke feels dizzy after sitting up quickly. What should Sasha do?
o: Help him dress quickly so that he can get some fresh air outside
Tell him this is normal and that he can leave when he is ready
Let him rest sitting, give him water, and stay until he is steady
Give him a cup of strong coffee and let him go home
questions.why: Dizziness on sitting up is common after lying relaxed. Let him sit still, give water and stay with him until he is steady; do not hurry him to stand, dress or leave.

questions.q: Which aftercare advice should Sasha give Mr. Clarke?
o: Take a very hot bath straight away to keep the muscles loose
Avoid drinking water, so that he does not need the toilet
Eat a large meal and have a drink straight after, to relax
Drink water, rest, and avoid alcohol and hard exercise
questions.why: Water and rest support the body after massage. Alcohol, heavy exercise and very hot baths straight afterwards can make a relaxed client feel faint.

questions.q: What is the difference between a contraindication and a contra-action?
o: A contraindication happens after a treatment; a contra-action is found before it
A contraindication stops a treatment; a contra-action is a reaction to it
A contraindication affects the therapist; a contra-action affects only the client
They are two words for the same thing, used by different therapists
questions.why: A contraindication is found in the consultation and stops or changes the treatment. A contra-action is an unwanted reaction that happens during or after the treatment.

questions.q: Which is the usual order of movements in a massage sequence?
o: Petrissage, then tapotement, then effleurage, and finally friction
Tapotement, then petrissage, then effleurage, then friction
Effleurage, petrissage, then friction or tapotement, then effleurage
Friction, then vibration, then tapotement, then petrissage
questions.why: Effleurage spreads the oil and warms the area, deeper movements follow, and effleurage returns to calm the area at the end.

questions.q: Which muscle lies on each side of the spine and holds the back upright?
o: Gastrocnemius
Deltoid
Trapezius
Erector spinae
questions.why: The erector spinae are the long muscles on each side of the spine that hold the back upright. The trapezius is across the upper back and neck, the deltoid covers the shoulder, and the gastrocnemius is the calf.
